# A. Prime Or Composite

## How to find it

Decompose `n-1` into an odd part and powers of two, then test the deterministic 64-bit witness set.

## Correctness

For prime inputs the strong Fermat chain condition holds for every base. The cited bounded witness theorem guarantees every composite below `2^64` fails at least one selected base.

## Complexity

`O(log n)` modular multiplications per base.

# B. Complete Factorization

## How to find it

Use Miller--Rabin as the stopping certificate and Pollard--rho only to split composite work items.

## Correctness

Each split preserves the product invariant. Every accepted leaf is prime, so termination yields exactly a prime factorization; sorting fixes the output order.

## Complexity

Expected roughly `O(n^(1/4))` per difficult factor discovery, with small memory.

# C. Large Totient

## How to find it

Factor first and apply the prime reduction once per distinct factor.

## Correctness

Inclusion--exclusion over divisibility by the distinct prime factors gives `n product (1-1/p)`.

## Complexity

Expected factorization time plus `O(number of prime factors)`.

# D. Large Divisor Statistics

## How to find it

For each prime power independently choose an exponent from zero through `e`.

## Correctness

Unique factorization makes these choices bijective with divisors. Counts multiply, and distributivity makes the geometric sums multiply.

## Complexity

Expected factorization time.
